Chapter 9: Healing Divisions, Building Unity
Every family, at some point, knows what it feels like to be divided. Maybe it’s a harsh word, a misunderstanding that spirals, or a wound that just won’t heal. The Church isn’t immune to this pain either.
In recent years, we’ve seen disagreements—over doctrine, liturgy, even leadership—leave people feeling isolated, or worse, betrayed. That sense of togetherness, which once felt so strong, can suddenly seem so fragile, threatened by suspicion and mistrust.
Picture a parish council meeting. Tensions run high as members argue over changes to the liturgy. Old friends, now standing on opposite sides, each one sure they’re protecting what matters most. What started as a conversation to bring everyone together, only seems to make the gap wider. Afterward, a few people linger in the parking lot, quietly wondering if things will ever feel normal again.
In moments like this, it’s easy to lose hope. You might even start to believe that unity is just out of reach. But here’s something important to remember—unity in the Church has never meant everyone has to look or think the same. It’s really about a shared commitment to Christ. It’s about choosing to bear with one another in love, especially when it’s tough.
So, where does healing begin? With humility. It’s that honest moment when you admit you don’t have all the answers, and you realize everyone needs a little grace. Healing means listening—not to win an argument, but to really understand where the other person is coming from. It means being willing to forgive, to let go of old hurts, and to reach for reconciliation, even when it feels risky.
Imagine a priest, exhausted after years of conflict, deciding to reach out to folks who left the parish. He listens to their stories, acknowledges their pain, and asks for forgiveness where he’s fallen short. Some people come back. Others don’t. But that act of reaching out—it becomes a turning point. It’s proof that healing really can happen.
Most of the time, nobody notices the tiny steps that build unity—a kind word, sharing a meal, or saying a prayer for someone you disagree with. These moments might seem quiet, but they’re incredibly powerful. They remind us that the Church isn’t just a bunch of factions. It’s a family, held together by a love that’s stronger than any argument.
The path to unity isn’t easy. It takes patience, courage, and a willingness to start over—sometimes more than once. But here’s the promise: wherever you find forgiveness, humility, and love, unity can be rebuilt. And that hope? It’s always worth holding onto.
